title: SWE-bench Multimodal v2 is not multimodal
text:
Contents Intro Methodology SWE Multimodal v2 Benchmark details Experiment details Removing Git history GPT-6 Luna xhigh runs Sample trace Sonnet 5.5 max runs Results GPT-6 Luna xhigh (480 tasks) Sonnet 5.5 max (60-task subset) Why did removing images make so little difference? Images were rarely required The hidden tests don't check what the images show The models may already know some fixes Example tasks where images were not needed MMMU-Pro as a control GPT-6 Luna xhigh (1730 questions) Sonnet 5.5 max (120 questions) Conclusion Acknowledgements Intro I was using SWE-bench Multimodal v2 to establish baselines for a project at the Prime Intellect residency. I found out that GPT-6 Luna (xhigh) performed similarly on the benchmark whether I used normal images or OCR-based output or no images at all. This felt unexpected for a multimodal benchmark. I wondered: does this mean the images are optional? After looking into the data, we found that most of the information the models needed was already in the issue text or derivable from the code. I also ran Sonnet 5.5 on a subset to check whether this was specific to Luna. Its score barely changed when I removed the images. In short, Removing the images barely changes the score, for both Luna and Sonnet Most tasks can be solved from the issue text and the code alone, since the images mostly repeat what the text already says The hidden tests rarely check details found only in the images, like the colours or spacing in a design spec, which helps explain why removing images barely affects the score What changes when the images disappear? with imagesno imageschange, points SWE-bench Multimodal v2 · resolved GPT-6 Luna xhigh 480 tasks 36.9% 37.1% +0.2 Sonnet 5.5 max 60 tasks 35.0% 40.0% +5.0 MMMU-Pro · accuracy GPT-6 Luna xhigh 1,730 questions 79.7% 36.9% −42.8 Sonnet 5.5 max 120 questions 80.8% 44.2% −36.6 Scores barely move on SWE-bench Multimodal, while accuracy falls sharply on MMMU-Pro. Each pair uses the same tasks within that experiment. Vals AI released a SWE-bench Multimodal v2 leaderboard on October 14, so this felt like a good time to write this blog up and share our findings. Methodology SWE Multimodal v2 Benchmark details The benchmark has 480 tasks built from GitHub issues in 11 JavaScript repos (Carbon alone accounts for 133), most with screenshots. 39 of the 480 have no image in the issue text at all. It's worth noting that even these tasks can involve images, since the agent may take screenshots to check its work or open image files already in the repo. Most tasks are small fixes to UI components, map rendering, syntax highlighting or Lighthouse audits, things like a missing aria-label, a misaligned icon or a keyword highlighted in the wrong colour. They are fairly focused and short horizon. Luna xhigh spent a median of 5.5 minutes on each. Vals AI reports 5min 14 sec median time for Luna and 24m+ for Sonnet 5.5 at max reasoning. I find it interesting that this benchmark is not saturated given the nature of tasks. Tasks per repo (click to expand) RepoTasks carbon-design-system/carbon133 openlayers/openlayers77 GoogleChrome/lighthouse54 bpmn-io/bpmn-js53 highlightjs/highlight.js39 PrismJS/prism38 alibaba-fusion/next36 grommet/grommet20 prettier/prettier13 eslint/eslint11 scratchfoundation/scratch-gui6 Experiment details I evaluated two models on SWE-bench Multimodal v2 and MMMU-Pro: Model SWE-bench Multimodal v2 MMMU-Pro Input conditions GPT-6 Luna (xhigh) All 480 tasks All 1,730 questions Images, OCR, no images Sonnet 5.5 (max) 60-task subset 120-question subset Images, no images For SWE-bench Multimodal, rollouts ran with full network isolation, and grading took place in a separate sandbox. Issue images were downloaded beforehand so they could be provided without network access. Removing Git history In the traces of an initial run, we caught agents: Searching Git history for commits associated with the reported issue or an upstream fix. Inspecting later commits and their diffs to retrieve the implementation that fixed the issue. Incorporating code from those upstream fixes into their submitted patches. As you can see, sometimes the agents take 'learn from the codebase' too literally. This is a known SWE-bench reward hack, documented about a year ago, and we were surprised to still see this in the benchmark images. Checking out an older commit takes the files back in time, but it doesn't erase newer commits from .git. So the agent may start with the buggy code while the actual upstream fix is still sitting in the same repository. It can go on an archaeological expedition through Git refs or stored objects, find the fix, and copy it instead of solving the issue. To prevent this, we rebuilt the benchmark images to keep only the task's base commit and the objects needed to reconstruct its files. We then copied the cleaned filesystem into a fresh image so the removed history couldn't survive in older image layers. GPT-6 Luna xhigh runs I was using GPT-6 Luna xhigh for ablations. There were three full runs on all 480 tasks, one per condition, on verifiers with the Codex harness. The three conditions were native image input, a custom OCR-based representation of each image and no images mode. This is possible to do in verifiers because of the interception server. It sits between the harness and the model API, letting us rewrite messages before the model sees them. I used it to replace images in both user messages and tool outputs with OCR text or placeholders. In OCR mode, each image is replaced by the text that OCR reads from it, with every word placed on a character grid at its position in the image and tagged with its colour. A header gives the image size and main colours, and a short list underneath describes shapes that are not text, such as icons, outlines and lines. The interceptor rewrites every image in each model request, in the issue and in tool outputs alike, before it reaches the model. Sample trace Issue message of task lighthouse-4036, which has 2 screenshots, as the model received it in each of the three modes. Swipe or scroll sideways, or jump to with images · with OCR · no images With images1 / 3 → With OCR← 2 / 3 → No images← 3 / 3 Full trace in the no images mode. Overall, it seems I can finalize with up to 10 lines. messageUpdated the rel="noopener" audit to ignore mailto: links, case-insensitively, in lighthouse-core/audits/dobetterweb/external-anchors-use-rel-noopener.js:50. Added lowercase and uppercase regression coverage in lighthouse-core/test/audits/dobetterweb/external-anchors-use-rel-noopener-test.js:69. Validation: all 5 focused audit tests pass. The model didn't need the screenshots here (a Lighthouse audit flagging the mailto link, and a broken link on Android). The issue title already says to ignore mailto links, and the audit already skipped javascript: links, so it just added mailto: next to that. Sonnet 5.5 max runs It was interesting to see that Claude models were ahead of all OpenAI models on the leaderboard, which made me pause and worry a bit. Maybe Luna just doesn't make good use of images, and a model that does would show a gap. I shared my concern with Florian and he suggested we could run Sonnet 5.5 as well. Vals AI's SWE-bench Multimodal leaderboard as of October 20. Sonnet 5.5 at max reasoning is slow and pricey, so I picked a 60-task subset. Those 60 tasks cost about $170, more than the whole 480-task Luna run (about $110, inference plus sandboxes). Sonnet runs at max effort (adaptive thinking) in the Claude Code harness, on 60 randomly sampled tasks spread over all 11 repos. The same tasks were used for both runs, native images and no images, with one rollout per task. No OCR run this time. The rest of the setup was the same as the Luna runs, except for the agent timeout limit, which was raised from 20 to 50 minutes since Vals AI reports Sonnet at max effort taking 24m+ per task. Results GPT-6 Luna xhigh (480 tasks) All three runs resolved 175 to 178 of 480 tasks (36.5 to 37.1%). This is in line with the 37.5% that Vals AI's SWE-bench Multimodal leaderboard reports for GPT-6 Luna on max effort (as of October 2026), even though they run it in a different harness (mini-swe-agent). Run Resolved Rate Native images 177 / 480 36.9% OCR text 175 / 480 36.5% No images 178 / 480 37.1% Pair Both resolved Only the first Only the second Both failed Images vs OCR 163 14 12 291 Images vs no images 167 10 11 292 OCR vs no images 161 14 17 288 157 tasks were resolved in all three runs and 284 failed in all three, so 441 of 480 (92%) got the same result every time. The remaining 39 change outcomes, with gains and losses roughly balancing out (images vs no images is −0.2 points, 95% CI −2.1 to +1.7, McNemar p = 1.0). Observations Some observations by my trace police (Sonnet 5.5, sometimes Opus 5.5 reviewer agents) after going through the traces: In the native and no-image runs, Luna's network lookups all failed, and most went looking for the upstream issue, PR or commit rather than the images. The only images it opened itself were rendering-test baselines from the repo. In the no-image run, Luna only now and then mentions the missing images in its thinking. When it does, it works around them ("Since I can't see the image, I should infer what the expected outcome is" on carbon-4431, "I can't access screenshot URLs since images are removed, and I respect that" on lighthouse-9151), and once in a while it guesses what an image shows. Otherwise it gets on with the issue text and the code. In the native-image run, Luna mostly ignores the images. Going by its reasoning summaries, it cites a specific visual detail in well under half the tasks that have images, and those tasks resolve just as often in the runs without images. Sonnet 5.5 max (60-task subset) Run Sonnet 5.5 max GPT-6 Luna xhigh on the same 60 Native images 21 / 60 (35.0%) 14 / 60 (23.3%) OCR text not run 10 / 60 (16.7%) No images 24 / 60 (40.0%) 14 / 60 (23.3%) 19 tasks were resolved in both Sonnet runs and 34 failed in both. 2 flipped towards images and 5 towards no images (−5 points, 95% CI roughly −15 to +5, McNemar p = 0.45). With only 60 tasks, this shows no sign of an image benefit but can't rule out a moderate one. Median thinking per task was 69k tokens with images and 67k without them. The no-image runs took a few more tool calls (median 82 vs 67) and a bit longer (18 vs 14 minutes). In contrast, Sonnet used 3x the output tokens on MMMU-Pro when images were gone. Observations Some observations by my trace police after going through the traces: In 27 of 60 no-image tasks Sonnet tried to get at the images or the upstream issue (curl, WebFetch, opening png files), with no luck. Funnily, the thinking often says "I can't see the image" and then guesses what it shows anyway. The guesses mostly restated the issue text, so they often matched the real image (27 of 46 guesses). Three guesses about images Sonnet never saw (click to expand) Thinking quotes are Anthropic's summarized thinking, not the raw chain of thought. All three guesses match the real image, and all three tasks still failed, with and without images. lighthouse-9451 The issue says "A page like the below should be visible during the offline pass, not the desktop version of the site." Looking at the screenshot description, the expected behavior is that during the offline pass the service worker should serve its offline fallback page, but the reporter saw the real desktop site loading instead. There is no screenshot description. The screenshot it never saw: grommet-5243 The issue says the checked background colour is applied to every radio button, not just the checked one. Sonnet's message after reproducing the bug: Bug reproduced: all three radio boxes get #3b5ed8, matching the screenshot in the issue. The screenshot it never saw: grommet-6296 The issue says a long string in the PageHeader heading "overflows and collides with other content". Without seeing the actual screenshot, I'm guessing the overflow is likely a long unbroken string in the heading, like a filename or email, pushing into the actions column. The screenshot it never saw: Sonnet kept trying to recall the upstream fix from memory. Reviewers flagged it in 38 of 60 no-image runs (it remembered Carbon's useIdPrefix and .bx--grid--narrow names, for example). It doesn't look like it was making up for the missing images though, since the native runs did it too. Where it needed to see the UI, it took its own headless Chrome screenshots. In the no-image run those came back as the placeholder too, so it measured bounding boxes and sampled pixels instead. Both conditions rendered the UI about equally often (34 runs with images, 33 without). In 5 rollouts, it refused to look up stuff upstream. Traces where it refused to look upstream (click to expand) These are Anthropic's summarized thinking, not the raw chain of thought. grommet-2695 Actually, in a SWE-bench-like setting, fetching the actual upstream patch would be closer to contamination than genuine problem-solving, and since I'm confident I can solve this from the repo alone, the cleaner approach is to skip the web lookup and trust my own analysis. highlight.js-2726 Still, I'm weighing whether this counts as contamination given a benchmark setting -- a human contributor would naturally check the issue tracker discussion, but if the goal is to solve purely from the issue text, pulling the upstream patch feels like cheating. prism-3372 I'm going to stick with my earlier decision not to look up the actual upstream Prism implementation or tests — that would feel like cheating. Why did removing images make so little difference? To check whether images were slipping through somewhere, I had the trace police inspect both models' runs and checked some samples myself. The audit found no issue images reaching either model in the no-image runs. The reviewers also assessed whether each task needed its images. For each task, they examined the native-image trace alongside the issue images, the merged fix and the hidden tests. These ratings are the reviewers' judgments and not definitive labels. Images were rarely requiredGPT-6 Luna xhigh In 403 of 480 tasks (84%) the issue text fully specifies the bug and the images only illustrate it. Resolution counts barely move across the three runs. The helpful category has nine resolutions in each run, and of the seven tasks rated required, only one was resolved, with native images. A lot of the Carbon issues come with detailed design spec screenshots (colours, spacing, icon placement), but the test that grades them is often just a snapshot of the component's prop types (carbon-13851, for example, comes with a full TimePicker error/warning spec, and the test only checks that two new props exist). The OpenLayers and bpmn-js issues have GIFs of the bug, while the tests check internal state like waypoints or function arguments. What the screenshot specifies // PublicAPI-test.js.snap, TimePicker props "value": Object { "type": "string", }, + "warning": Object { + "type": "bool", + }, + "warningText": Object { + "type": "node", + }, Everything the grader checks The test only checks that warning and warningText exist as props. The red border, the icons, the message colours and the 8px and 16px spacing are never checked. When tasks failed, it was usually because the tests expected some detail that neither the text nor the images mention, like an exact prop name, null vs undefined, or something settled in the GitHub issue comments that the model never sees. The reviewers flagged this in all but 2 of the Luna failures they reviewed, and in 32 of Sonnet's 36 no-image failures. I haven't checked every case by hand. For the images to matter, a test would have to check something you can only learn from them, like which component is broken or a value from the design spec. The models may already know some fixes Memorisation is another possibility. These tasks come from public GitHub issues and PRs from 2017–2024, so both models may already know some of the fixes and have little need for the screenshots. In fact, Sonnet tried to recall the upstream fix in 38 of 60 no-image runs. Example tasks where images were not needed These ten tasks were resolved with native images, OCR text and no images. MMMU-Pro makes a good control because it isn't agentic. It's single-turn multiple-choice questions across college subjects, with no repo to read and no tools to fall back on. In its standard split, each question comes with a diagram, chart or photo that carries information the text does not restate, so a model that cannot see the image should actually lose points there. Without images, Sonnet uses about three times as many output tokens (6.8k to 19.8k). They say a picture is worth a thousand words. Apparently, removing one adds several thousand for Sonnet. It says it can't see the image in 78 of the 120 questions and openly guesses in 92, often from the answer options themselves. Opus 5.5 reviewers trace 55 of the 67 misses in the no-image run to the missing image. Conclusion The experiments show that SWE-bench Multimodal v2 scores were largely insensitive to removing image inputs in our setups, while the same ablation cost both models around 40 points on MMMU-Pro. The audit points to two reasons. Screenshots often repeat what the issue text already says, and the hidden tests rarely check visual requirements. Thanks for reading!
